messages.subject: Fit Measures in DWLS
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for all of the great work. This package is phenomenal.

I have recently been reading that CFi and perhaps some other fit measures are not appropriate in DWLS, or at least the traditional cutoff values reported by Hu & Bentler are not appropriate for models estimated by DWLS. For a nice review of what has been written I will refer people to methods section of a free article published in PLOS One: http://www.plosone.org/article/info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0061191

The above article takes the approach of using RMSEA and RMSR to assess model fit (both of which lavaan supplies), applying Hu and Bentler Criteria. However, it seems that other fit measures can also be used. For example, SAS modifies the GFI for WLS and DWLS ( http://www.math.wpi.edu/saspdf/stat/chap19.pdf page 539).

Does lavaan use a special estimation procedures for GFI in cases of DWLS, or does it simply apply the same GFI estimation procedure to all estimators?

Also, is there a preferred index of model fit with DWLS in lavaan?

-Paul

messages.subject_clean: Merging data imputed datasets by imputation number and ID
messages.body_plain:
If I understand correctly, you have 2 different Amelia objects, one for each sex.  They don't contain the same people/observations, so you don't really need to merge the data by any variables, you just need to stack them.  I assume the imputed data sets for each sex have the same column names in the same order, and that you have included the sex indicator in the "id" argument in amelia(..., id = "sex", ...) so that this variable is still included in the imputed data sets even though it is not used in the imputation model.  You can use the same type of loop in the mi.meld() example to create a list of stack data sets:

nImps <- 5
maleImputations <- amelia(maleData, n = nImps, id = "sex", ...)
female Imputations <- amelia(femaleData, n = nImps, id = "sex", ...)

## create an empty list to populate
stackedImps <- list(NULL)

## populate the list in a loop
for (i in 1:nImps) {
  stackedImps[[i]] <- rbind(maleImputations$imputations[[i]], femaleImputations$imputations[[i]])
}

Then you can feed the stackedImps list as the data argument to runMI()

FYI, you can also include sex as the cross-sectional variable in amelia(..., cs = "sex", ...), but it isn't the same as Enders' (2010) example.

Terry

messages.subject: Re: Fit Measures in DWLS
messages.body_plain:
On 05/01/2013 04:34 PM, Paul Gerrard wrote:

> The above article takes the approach of using RMSEA and RMSR to assess
> model fit (both of which lavaan supplies), applying Hu and Bentler
> Criteria. However, it seems that other fit measures can also be used.
> For example, SAS modifies the GFI for WLS and DWLS
> ( http://www.math.wpi.edu/saspdf/stat/chap19.pdf page 539).

The SAS manual shows two different equations, but the upper one can be
rewritten as the lower one (given an appropriate choice for W). So there
is really only one definition of GFI, for all estimators.

> Does lavaan use a special estimation procedures for GFI in cases of
> DWLS, or does it simply apply the same GFI estimation procedure to all
> estimators?

lavaan uses one approach for all estimators; from the source code in
fit.Measures.R (for single group 'g'):

wls.diff <- wls.obs - wls.est
t1 <- crossprod(wls.diff, wls.v) %*% wls.diff
t2 <- crossprod(wls.obs, wls.v) %*% wls.obs
gfi.group[g] <- 1 - t1/t2

where wls.v is computed differently depending on the estimator

wls.v <- lavaan:::getWLS.V(fit)[[g]]

and g is the group number.

Yves.

I think the issue might be in the starting values that are being used. Alex

anticipate ;-)

constraints. It makes no distinction between highly complex nonlinear
constraints, and simple linear constraints. This will change in the

constrained optimization techniques if the constraints are linear.

Hi Bill,

There are no problems with your model specification or your call to Amelia.  The reason you see the warnings is because it is a saturated model.  Saturated models have a chi-squared value of zero, which is all well and good, but they also have zero degrees of freedom.  So when runMI() tries to combine the chi-squared values, it is making a call to calculate the probabilities (p values) of observing the chi-squared or F value when df = 0, which is undefined.  However, notice that all the warnings concern calls to pf() and pchisq(), so that is the only issue.  You models were estimated and parameters combined successfully:

  Degrees of freedom                                 0
  P-value (Chi-square)                           1.000

Parameter estimates:

                   Estimate  Std.err  Z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
Regressions:

For example, the parameter estimates from a CFA model can be used as starting values for a multitrait-multimethod model. The compareFit function is also added to build a template for comparing multiple nested and nonnested models in a nice table format. You didn't provide any information about your data or model, but my first guess is that your model is saturated, i.e., there are just as many parameters being estimated as there are observed means, variances, and covariances. messages.body_plain:
Hi Kathleen, Yves, and Jarrett,

Unless I misunderstood the question, I have to disagree with Jarrett.

If the CFAs are nested (e.g., CFA1 uses all the variables and CFA 2 uses a subset of those), you can compare your CFAs using X2 tests, AIC, and BIC.

If the models are not nested (e.g., CFA1 uses variables 1-6 and CFA 2 uses variables 4-10), which I think is similar to your situation, you should not use X2 tests (they are only appropriate for nested model comparisons), but you can use AIC/BIC. AIC/BIC are appropriate for both nested and non-nested situations (e.g., see Burnham et al. 2011. Behav Ecol Sociobiol (2011) 65:23–35).

In both situations, you can also compare the models with the more descriptive statistics, like CLI and TLI.

Best,
James

This is indeed the case (at least in 0.5-13 and older). Explicit
constraints (using the constraints argument) are handled by the
'constrained' optimizer (nlminb.constr), which is much more sensitive to
starting values than the unconstrained optimizer (nlminb).

If you can, it is always better to use the 'same label, same value'
trick in the model syntax. Here, we simply reduce the dimension of the
parameter space and apply unconstrained optimization. Much faster, much
more stable.

One day, lavaan will 'detect' simple equality constraints provided by
the 'constraints' argument, and handle them accordingly.

messages.subject: McDonald's NCI
messages.body_plain:
This message is more for Yves, but others might be interested.

I am wondering if it would be possible to add McDonald's (1989) Non-centrality Index as one of the options in the fitMeasures() function. I have written a homemade function that will use the innards of a fitted lavaan model and produce the index, but it would be easier if if were an option. I pasted my function below in case it might be of interest to other users and/or make adding the Mc to lavaan easier.

#Function to calculate McDonald's NCI
Mc <- function (object, digits=3){
fit <- inspect(object, "fit") # lavaan's default output
chisq <- unlist(fit["chisq"]) #model Chi-square
df <- unlist(fit["df"]) # model df
n <- object@SampleStats@ntotal
ncp <- max(chisq - df,0)  #non-centrality parameter
d <- ncp/(n-1)  #scaled non-centrality parameter
#McDonald's non-centrality index
Mc <- exp((d)*-.5)
#Print the value
Mc
}

# Example Use
HS.model<-'visual =~x1+x2+x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
Mc(fit)

McDonald, R. P. (1989). An index of goodness-of-fit based on noncentrality. Journal of Classification, 6(1), 97-103. doi: 10.1007/bf01908590

Best,

Alex

messages.body_plain:
James,

What you are saying is true for parameter nesting, but only applies when the parameters estimate relationships among the same set of variables.  I think you may have confused parameter nesting with variables nesting (although I have never heard of a mention of variable nesting in practice because models that explain different data are typically not compared).  As an extreme example, consider a situation in which we fit a saturated model to 3 variables, and fit another saturated model to 2 of those 3 variables.  The log-likelihood differs between the two saturated models, as do the AIC and BIC.

> HS.model <- ' x1 ~~ x2 + x3 ; x2 ~~ x3'
> fit123 <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
> HS.model <- ' x1 ~~ x2'
> fit12 <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
> sapply(list(X.1.2.and.3 = fit123, X.1.and.2 = fit12), function(x) c(AIC = AIC(x), BIC = BIC(x)))
    X.1.2.and.3 X.1.and.2
AIC    2725.955  1876.066
BIC    2748.197  1887.188

The question is:  What sense would it make to say that the saturated model fit to variables {x1, x2} fits better than the saturated model fit to variables {x1, x2, x3}, when both models fit perfectly?  I think this might conceptually similar to other situations in which you would not compare results that do not share a common basis for comparison.  For example, in a 2-way ANOVA with gender and treatment as predictors, you would not compare the male treatment group to the female control group because you have no way of knowing whether any differences are due to gender or treatment.  Or if you were comparing the proportion of people who would vote Republican or Democrat, but you use a different denominator for each proportion:
P_Republicans =  N_Republicans / (N_Republicans + N_Democrats)
P_Democrats=  N_Democrats/ (N_Republicans + N_Democrats + N_Independents)
Terry

I just came back to a script that I worked on last year (using a version of lavaan in the 0.4-* family), and it no longer works. However, the results show that the lower-order factor variances are being fixed to 1 instead of 0 (see parameters in rows 9 and 10 of parameter table).

I have also attached the data file and the R syntax.  I would guess that this is a bug, simply because the parameters are being fixed to different values than what the parameter table says.  But since they have to do with phantom variables, I wonder whether there is simply some default that is not being overridden by the syntax.
